extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary students, and general readers of Emerson
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and extraction of prescriptive criteria Emerson gives about the poet, imagination, and art in his essay 'Experience'. Useful for aspiring poets, literary critics, and readers seeking Emerson's standards for poetic thought and temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformative imagination (use of tropes and symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The use of symbols has a certain power of emancipation and exhilaration for all men... We are like persons who come out of a cave or cellar into the open air. This is the effect on us of tropes, fables, oracles, and all poetic forms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson gives many examples of metaphoric/metamorphic definitions (Aristotle's space, Plato's line, Vitruvius on anatomy, biblical and classical imagery) to show how a poet's tropes reveal another world and free perception. The power to metamorphose ordinary things into signs of larger truths is a central mark of imaginative success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as liberator — imaginative work should emancipate readers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poets are thus liberating gods... An imaginative book renders us much more service at first, by stimulating us through its tropes..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson emphasizes the emotion of joy and exhilaration that imaginative metamorphosis produces in readers; successful poetry unlocks chains, admits new scenes, and gives readers a 'new sense' of the world. Early, affective stimulation can be as important as later precise sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / departure from routine
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the value which attaches to Pythagoras, Paracelsus, Cornelius Agrippa...is the certificate we have of departure from routine, and that here is a new witness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strangeness, unconventional claims, or eccentric cosmologies (angels, magic, astrology, etc.) are valuable chiefly as evidence the thinker departs from routine and brings a new witness. Emerson prizes the radical, the new vision, even when its literal facts are questionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity of conviction — 'inflamed' thought
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a man is inflamed and carried away by his thought, to that degree that he forgets the authors and the public and heeds only this one dream which holds him like an insanity, let me read his paper..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson favors work produced from an obsessive, single-minded inward compulsion. The sign of worth is the author's being overtaken by the thought (forgetting audience, sources), not polished eclecticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold symbols lightly; avoid fixed mysticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mysticism consists in the mistake of an accidental and individual symbol for an universal one... The mystic must be steadily told,--All that you say is just as true without the tedious use of that symbol as with it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: nailing one private symbol as if universal. Good practice: translate private symbols into equivalents others use; prefer universal signs (Emerson: 'a little algebra') rather than idiosyncratic, permanent fetishized symbols. Be willing to rephrase symbols into common terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluidity of imagination — symbols must flow, not freeze
rubrics_metrics.description: "But the quality of the imagination is to flow, and not to freeze. The poet did not stop at the color or the form, but read their meaning..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols and metaphors should remain dynamic and convertible. Stasis (fixing a trope eternally) turns imagination into error; the creative faculty is valued for its continual metamorphosis and translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and scope of thought; using nature as exponent
rubrics_metrics.description: "All books of the imagination endure, all which ascend to that truth that the writer sees nature beneath him, and uses it as his exponent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endurance comes from works that perceive truth beneath surface nature and deploy nature as an exponent of larger ideas. Emerson treats such transcendental reach as the mark of immortal sentences or verses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and compulsion in creation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Doubt not, O poet, but persist. Say 'It is in me, and shall out.' ... Stand and strive, until at last rage draw out of thee that dream-power..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson prescribes stubbornness in the face of hooting and failure. The creative act is driven by an imperative within the artist; persistence through obscurity and derision is a criterion of eventual poetic fulfillment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and abundance of imaginative repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the creatures by pairs and by tribes pour into his mind...the rich poets...have obviously no limits to their works except the limits of their lifetime, and resemble a mirror carried through the street, ready to render an image of every created thing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poets manifest an inexhaustible store of images and subjects; their work is capacious, able to mirror 'every created thing.' Lack of repertoire or narrowness is a limitation; abundance is a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the living times and national material
rubrics_metrics.description: "We do not with sufficient plainness or sufficient profoundness address ourselves to life, nor dare we chaunt our own times and social circumstance...Banks and tariffs, the newspaper and caucus...are yet unsung."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson calls for poets to take their country's social, political, and material life as poetic material rather than shying away. Using immediate/national subjects (even apparently banal ones) with imaginative force is a mark of apt poetry for Emerson's context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive literariness or over-literalness
rubrics_metrics.description: "When we adhere to the ideal of the poet, we have our difficulties even with Milton and Homer. Milton is too literary, and Homer too literal and historical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson warns against extremes: being merely 'literary' (overcultivated style) or too literal/historical. The ideal poet achieves a balance—universalizing rather than merely ornamenting or documenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renunciation to the Muse — seclusion and humble devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thou shalt leave the world, and know the muse only...Thou shalt pass for a fool and a churl for a long season...This is the screen and sheath in which Pan has protected his well-beloved flower..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson presents renunciation and withdrawal from ordinary social pursuits as an explanatory condition of genuine poetic work. The social cost (being mocked, obscure) is part of the discipline; the reward is an inner ideal becoming real to the poet.
